# Editorial overview

## Read before code: problem dossiers

**A. Deadline Profit.** Sort unit jobs by deadline and retain selected profits in
a min-heap. After a deadline `d`, more than `d` jobs cannot fit; deleting the
least profitable keeps the best feasible set of that size. Test equal deadlines
and a high-profit late job. Time `O(n log n)`.

**B. Minimum Interval Cover.** At the leftmost uncovered point, choose among
available intervals the one reaching farthest right. Exchange any optimal
cover's first interval for this choice without reducing reach. Test a gap,
touching endpoints, and an interval that starts too late. Time `O(n log n)`.

**C. MST Savings.** Sum all edges, then use Kruskal/DSU to retain only
component-merging edges. The cut property proves their weight is minimum; the
difference is removable savings. Test a disconnected graph and parallel edges.

## Problem-specific proof map

**A. Deadline Profit.** After jobs are sorted by deadline, keep chosen profits
in a min-heap. If more jobs than available slots are kept, deleting the least
profitable one preserves the best total profit among feasible choices.

**B. Minimum Interval Cover.** At the current uncovered point, an optimal cover
can be exchanged to use an available interval reaching at least as far as the
greedy choice. Repeating this reaches the target with the fewest intervals.

**C. MST Savings.** Kruskal keeps exactly edges that join different components.
The cut property proves those edges form a minimum spanning tree; total weight
minus its weight is the maximum removable saving.

## Detailed solution guide

**A. Scheduling with Deadlines.** Sort jobs by deadline and keep the selected
profits in a min-heap. After considering all jobs with deadline at most `d`, the
heap contains the best set of jobs that can fit into `d` slots. If adding a job
creates too many selected jobs, remove the smallest profit. This exchange is
safe because any feasible schedule with the low-profit job can replace it by
the higher-profit job without using more time.

**B. Interval Cover.** To cover a target segment, repeatedly among all intervals
starting at or before the current uncovered point choose the one with farthest
right endpoint. Any valid solution must choose some interval covering the
current point; choosing the farthest-reaching such interval cannot make the
remaining suffix harder to cover.

**C. Kruskal Savings.** Sort edges by weight and add an edge only if it connects
two different components. The DSU maintains the connected components of the
partial forest. The cut property proves each chosen edge is safe: it is the
lightest available edge crossing some cut. Savings are total edge weight minus
the MST weight.

**Common pitfalls.** Greedy proofs need an exchange or cut argument, not just
intuition. For deadline scheduling, deadlines are capacities. For interval
cover, detect gaps when no candidate reaches the current point.

The three greedy solutions use exchange arguments.

- A keeps the highest-profit feasible set of unit jobs by deadline using a
  min-heap.
- B repeatedly chooses, among intervals that already reach the uncovered
  point, the one extending farthest right.
- C is Kruskal's algorithm: add an edge exactly when it connects two DSU
  components, then compute removable weight.

Each proof compares the greedy choice with an optimal solution and shows the
greedy choice can be exchanged in without worsening feasibility or objective.

# A. Deadline Profit

## Restatement

Each unit job has deadline and profit. Maximize profit.

## Observations and algorithm

Sort jobs by deadline. After reading every job with deadline at most `d`, keep
the selected profits in a min-heap. If its size exceeds `d`, delete its least
profitable job: no schedule can complete more than `d` unit jobs by that time.
For `(1,5),(1,2),(2,4)`, discard profit `2` and keep `5,4`.

```text
sort by deadline; push each profit; if heap.size > deadline: pop minimum
```

## Correctness proof

The heap has maximum total profit among feasible selected sets of its size. A
violating set must discard one job; removing the minimum profit loses least
value, preserving optimality by induction. `\square`

## Complexity

Sorting and heap operations take `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` memory. In Python
use `heapq`; test equal deadlines and a job with deadline zero if allowed.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n;if(!(cin>>n))return 0;vector<pair<int,int>>j(n);for(auto&x:j)cin>>x.first>>x.second;sort(j.begin(),j.end());priority_queue<int,vector<int>,greater<int>>pq;for(auto[d,p]:j){pq.push(p);if((int)pq.size()>d)pq.pop();}long long s=0;while(!pq.empty()){s+=pq.top();pq.pop();}cout<<s<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys,heapq
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    n=data[0]; jobs=sorted((data[i],data[i+1]) for i in range(1,2*n+1,2)); h=[]
    for d,p in jobs:
        heapq.heappush(h,p)
        if len(h)>d: heapq.heappop(h)
    print(sum(h))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# B. Minimum Interval Cover

## Restatement

Minimum intervals needed to cover `[0,T]`, or `-1`.

## Observations and algorithm

Sort intervals by left endpoint. At current covered point `cur`, scan every
interval beginning no later than `cur` and choose the greatest right endpoint.
If none extends beyond `cur`, coverage is impossible. Trace `[0,2],[1,5],[4,6]`
to choose reach 2, then 5, then 6.

```text
while cur<T: best=max right among starts<=cur; fail if best==cur; cur=best
```

## Correctness proof

Every valid cover must choose an interval reaching the current uncovered point.
Replacing its first such interval by the farthest-reaching greedy interval
cannot reduce coverage of the remaining suffix, proving an exchange step. `\square`

## Complexity

The sort dominates: `O(n log n)` time, `O(n)` memory. Test a gap, touching
endpoints, and one interval already covering the whole target.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int T,n;if(!(cin>>T>>n))return 0;vector<pair<int,int>>s(n);for(auto&x:s)cin>>x.first>>x.second;sort(s.begin(),s.end());int i=0,cur=0,ans=0;while(cur<T){int best=cur;while(i<n&&s[i].first<=cur)best=max(best,s[i++].second);if(best==cur){cout<<-1<<'\n';return 0;}cur=best;ans++;}cout<<ans<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    T,n=data[0],data[1]; seg=sorted((data[i],data[i+1]) for i in range(2,2+2*n,2)); i=ans=0; cur=0
    while cur<T:
        best=cur
        while i<n and seg[i][0]<=cur: best=max(best,seg[i][1]); i+=1
        if best==cur: print(-1); return
        cur=best; ans+=1
    print(ans)
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# C. MST Savings

## Restatement

Print total edge weight removable while keeping the graph connected, or `-1`.

## Observations and algorithm

Sum all edges, then process edges by weight with DSU. Add an edge only when its
endpoints are in different components; otherwise it would form a cycle. The
kept weight is the MST, so total minus kept is removable weight.

## Correctness proof

By the cut property, each lightest component-joining edge is safe for some MST.
After `n-1` accepted edges the forest is connected and minimum; fewer means the
input graph was disconnected. `\square`

## Complexity

Kruskal costs `O(m log m)` time and `O(n)` DSU memory. Use `long long` totals;
test parallel edges, equal weights, and a disconnected graph.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n,m;if(!(cin>>n>>m))return 0;vector<array<int,3>>e;long long total=0;for(int i=0,a,b,w;i<m;i++){cin>>a>>b>>w;e.push_back({w,a-1,b-1});total+=w;}vector<int>p(n);iota(p.begin(),p.end(),0);function<int(int)>f=[&](int x){return p[x]==x?x:p[x]=f(p[x]);};sort(e.begin(),e.end());long long keep=0;int cnt=0;for(auto [w,a,b]:e){a=f(a);b=f(b);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;keep+=w;cnt++;}}cout<<(cnt==n-1?total-keep:-1)<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    n,m=data[0],data[1]; edges=[]; total=0; idx=2
    for _ in range(m):
        a,b,w=data[idx],data[idx+1],data[idx+2]; idx+=3; edges.append((w,a-1,b-1)); total+=w
    p=list(range(n))
    def f(x):
        while p[x]!=x: p[x]=p[p[x]]; x=p[x]
        return x
    keep=0; cnt=0
    for w,a,b in sorted(edges):
        ra,rb=f(a),f(b)
        if ra!=rb: p[ra]=rb; keep+=w; cnt+=1
    print(total-keep if cnt==n-1 else -1)
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```
